reasons: Lake record is verified and identifies United States v. Harris as a U.S. Supreme Court case decided 1971-06-28.
Lake official citation is 403 U.S. 573, parallel citations are 91 S. Ct. 2075 and 29 L. Ed. 2d 723, and vendor-neutral citation is 1971 U.S. LEXIS 18.

The opinion frames the case as addressing the showing necessary to satisfy a magistrate that there is a substantial basis for crediting an informant's report in the search-warrant probable-cause setting.
The judgment reversed the Court of Appeals and reinstated the conviction after concluding the affidavit supported probable cause.
residual_risks: No separate Probable Cause home-page taxonomy file is disclosed; this review verifies semantic fit from the Harris opinion only.

defect.evidence_quote: MR. CHIEF JUSTICE BURGER announced the judgment of the Court and an opinion in which MR. JUSTICE BLACK and MR. JUSTICE BLACKMUN join, and in Part I of which MR. JUSTICE STEWART joins, and in Part III of which MR. JUSTICE WHITE joins.
defect.problem: The proposition is overframed as the case holding and includes an inexact embedded quote. The reputation point comes from Part II, joined only by the Chief Justice, Black, and Blackmun; Part III's penal-interest rationale was joined by the Chief Justice, Black, Blackmun, and White, while Stewart joined only Part I and the judgment. The quoted phrase is also not character-faithful because the opinion says the phrase followed by an em dash before 'sufficient,' not a comma inside the quote.
defect.proposed_fix: State the result and rationale with vote-sensitive limits: the Court reversed; a plurality plus Justice White treated the informant's admission of repeated illicit purchases at the premises as supporting probable cause; the officer-reputation point should be labeled plurality-only or omitted from the holding. Correct the quoted punctuation.

reasons: The opinion text supports that Part III says admissions of crime carry indicia of credibility and can support probable cause in this factual setting.
The opinion text does not support treating the officer-reputation rationale as a majority holding because it appears outside Part III.
The embedded quote in the payload has 'credibility,' but the disclosed opinion text has 'carry their own indicia of credibilitysufficient at least to support a finding of probable cause to search.'
residual_risks: A later treatment/currency assessment may still support the penal-interest principle as good law, but that does not cure the vote-count and quote-fidelity defect in this holding statement.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: Limit the holding to the warrant's validity and the Part III penal-interest rationale, with a plurality/concurrence caveat.

reasons: The case concerns a search warrant issued solely on an investigator's affidavit and whether the affidavit supplied probable cause.
The opinion repeatedly analyzes the facts and statements an affidavit must present to allow a magistrate to assess informant reliability.
residual_risks: No separate home-page taxonomy file is disclosed; this review verifies only that Harris materially relates to probable cause in affidavits.

reasons: Lake identity identifies the court as U.S. Supreme Court with court_level scotus.
For a federal search-and-seizure corpus, the SCOTUS source supports the weight label Binding — SCOTUS.
residual_risks: Lens A does not audit current treatment beyond support for the weight label.

reasons: The payload's treatment fields match the lake treatment fields: field_i_validity good_law, as_of_content 1971-06-28, as_of_treatment 2026-06-30, composite_basis migration-seed, composite_basis_ref United States v. Harris (1971), varies_by_point false, and the same scope note.
Treatment/currency is outside lens A, so no treatment finding is raised.
residual_risks: Lens B owns whether the treatment conclusion is current and complete.
